title: Apply pest control practices in ornamental plant production and landscaping

lessons.title: Know the pests and diseases
lessons.html:
What is a pest?

A pest is any living thing that damages plants: insects, mites, snails, slugs, rodents, and diseases caused by fungi, bacteria and viruses. Weeds are also pests because they compete for water, light and food. In a nursery or garden, pests spoil plants so they cannot be sold or look bad to the client.

Common pests

PestWhat you see
AphidsSmall green or black soft insects on new tips; sticky leaves
MealybugWhite, cottony insects in leaf joints
ScaleSmall brown or white bumps stuck to stems and leaves
Red spider miteTiny mites under leaves, fine webs, speckled pale leaves; worse in hot dry weather
WhiteflyTiny white flies that rise when you shake the plant
Snails and slugsHoles in leaves, slime trails, worse after rain
Caterpillars (e.g. lily borer on clivias and amaryllis)Chewed leaves, droppings

Common diseases

  • Powdery mildew – white powder on leaves.
  • Rust – orange-brown spots under leaves.
  • Black spot – black spots on rose leaves, which turn yellow and fall.
  • Damping off – seedlings collapse at the soil line.
  • Root rot – wilting plant in wet soil, brown soft roots.

Scouting

Walk through the plants regularly, as your supervisor sets. Look under leaves, on new tips and in leaf joints. Use a hand lens for mites. Write down what you find, where, and how bad it is. Early finding means easier control.

lessons.title: Integrated pest management and safe chemical use
lessons.html:
Integrated pest management (IPM)

IPM means using several methods together and only using chemicals when needed.

  • Cultural – healthy plants, right spacing, correct watering (not late in the day), clean pots and media, removing weeds and dead material.
  • Physical – picking off snails and caterpillars, yellow sticky traps for whitefly, washing aphids off with water, pruning out diseased parts.
  • Biological – using natural enemies such as ladybirds, lacewings and predatory mites. Some nurseries buy predatory mites.
  • Chemical – pesticides, only when the other methods are not enough.

Using pesticides safely

In South Africa, pesticides must be registered under the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947. The label is the law: use the product only for the pests and plants on the label, at the rate on the label.

  1. Only spray if you are trained and your supervisor has told you to.
  2. Read the label: rate, PPE, re-entry time and first aid.
  3. Wear the PPE on the label: usually overalls, chemical gloves, boots, goggles or face shield, and a respirator if required.
  4. Mix outdoors or in a ventilated area, on a level surface, away from water sources.
  5. Spray in calm weather, early or late. Never spray when it is windy or rain is about to fall.
  6. Keep people and animals out of the area for the re-entry time on the label.
  7. Triple-rinse empty containers, puncture them and return them for safe disposal as your farm requires. Never reuse them.
  8. Wash yourself and your PPE after spraying. Record the product, rate, date, area and your name.

Never

  • Never eat, drink or smoke while handling pesticides.
  • Never blow out a blocked nozzle with your mouth.
  • Never pour leftover chemical into drains, rivers or dams.

If someone is poisoned: remove them from the area, take off contaminated clothing, follow the first-aid steps on the label, and get medical help immediately. Take the label with you.

Key points

  • Scout often and record pests early.
  • IPM combines cultural, physical, biological and chemical control.
  • Pesticides are registered under Act 36 of 1947; follow the label.
  • Wear the PPE on the label and spray only in calm weather.
  • Never reuse containers or pour chemicals into water.
